questions.stem: What distinguishes semantic, instance and panoptic segmentation?
choices: They differ only in output resolution
Semantic labels every pixel by class without separating objects; instance separates individual objects; panoptic does both, assigning every pixel a class and, for countable things, an instance
Semantic is for video, instance for images
Panoptic is semantic segmentation at higher resolution
questions.explanation: Semantic segmentation cannot tell two adjacent cars apart — both are simply 'car' pixels. Instance segmentation separates them but traditionally ignores amorphous regions like sky or road. Panoptic unifies the two, covering both countable things and uncountable stuff.

questions.stem: Why does a segmentation network use an encoder-decoder structure?
choices: To reduce the parameter count
The encoder downsamples to build semantic context, and the decoder upsamples back to input resolution so a label can be assigned per pixel
Encoders handle colour, decoders handle shape
To allow two GPUs to be used
questions.explanation: Dense prediction needs both meaning and resolution. Downsampling grows the receptive field enough to recognise what something is, but destroys the spatial precision needed to say exactly where. The decoder recovers resolution, which is why the shape is universal in segmentation.

questions.stem: What do U-Net's skip connections carry, and why do they matter?
choices: Gradients only
High-resolution spatial detail from encoder layers directly to the matching decoder stage, recovering boundary precision that downsampling destroyed
The class labels
The loss values
questions.explanation: Without skips, the decoder must hallucinate fine boundaries from a coarse bottleneck, and edges come out blurred. Concatenating the encoder's high-resolution features restores the detail while the bottleneck supplies semantics. It is why U-Net remains strong on boundary-critical tasks like biomedical imaging.

questions.stem: Segmentation outputs show a regular checkerboard pattern. What is the cause and the usual fix?
choices: The input images are compressed; use PNG
Transposed convolution with a stride that does not divide the kernel size produces uneven output overlap; use bilinear upsampling followed by a regular convolution instead
The learning rate is too high; reduce it
Batch normalisation is missing
questions.explanation: When kernel size is not divisible by stride, some output positions receive contributions from more input positions than their neighbours, producing periodic intensity variation. Resize-then-convolve avoids the uneven overlap entirely, which is why most modern decoders use it.

questions.stem: Why is Dice loss often used instead of, or alongside, pixel-wise cross-entropy?
choices: Dice trains faster
Cross-entropy averages over pixels, so a tiny foreground is swamped by background; Dice measures region overlap and stays sensitive when the positive class is rare
Dice works only on binary masks
Cross-entropy cannot be used for segmentation
questions.explanation: In a scan where a lesion is 0.5% of pixels, a model predicting all background reaches 99.5% pixel accuracy and a low cross-entropy. Dice is a ratio of overlap to total area, so predicting nothing scores zero. The two are often summed to get stable gradients and imbalance robustness together.

questions.stem: How is mean IoU computed for semantic segmentation?
choices: The average IoU of all predicted boxes
Per class, intersection over union of predicted and true pixel sets, averaged across classes
The fraction of correctly classified pixels
The Dice coefficient divided by two
questions.explanation: Because it averages per class rather than per pixel, mIoU refuses to let abundant classes hide failure on rare ones. A model perfect on road and sky but useless on pedestrians scores poorly, which is exactly the behaviour you want from a segmentation metric.

questions.stem: Pixel accuracy is 97% but mean IoU is 0.41. What does this tell you?
choices: The model is excellent
A few large classes dominate the pixel count and are predicted well, while smaller or rarer classes are being missed — the mismatch is the point of using mIoU
The metric is computed wrongly
The images are too small
questions.explanation: Road, sky and building can be 90% of pixels in a street scene. Getting them right yields high pixel accuracy regardless of performance on poles, signs or pedestrians. The per-class IoU table is where you find which classes are failing.

questions.stem: How does Mask R-CNN extend Faster R-CNN?
choices: It replaces the backbone with a transformer
It adds a parallel branch predicting a binary mask for each detected region, alongside the existing class and box heads
It removes the region proposal network
It segments before detecting
questions.explanation: Mask R-CNN keeps detection intact and adds a small fully convolutional mask head per region of interest. Because masks are predicted per instance within a detected box, instances are separated by construction — the detection stage does that work.

questions.stem: What problem does RoIAlign solve that RoIPool does not?
choices: It runs faster
RoIPool quantises region boundaries to the feature grid, introducing misalignment of up to a stride; RoIAlign samples with bilinear interpolation, preserving sub-pixel correspondence
It handles more classes
It removes the need for anchors
questions.explanation: Rounding a region's coordinates to integer feature cells shifts the sampled region by up to half a stride — tolerable for a coarse class label, damaging for a pixel-accurate mask. RoIAlign avoids quantisation entirely and was the single change that made accurate instance masks work.

questions.stem: What does atrous spatial pyramid pooling contribute in DeepLab?
choices: It reduces parameters
It applies parallel dilated convolutions at several rates, capturing context at multiple scales without losing resolution
It replaces the decoder
It normalises the features
questions.explanation: Objects appear at many scales, and a single receptive field suits only one. ASPP probes the same feature map at several dilation rates simultaneously and fuses the results, gathering multi-scale context while keeping the spatial resolution that dense prediction needs.

questions.stem: What is promptable segmentation, as in the Segment Anything model?
choices: Segmenting based on a text description only
Producing a mask from a user-supplied prompt such as a point, box or rough mask, without the class being fixed in advance
Segmenting every image in a folder automatically
Asking a language model to describe the mask
questions.explanation: SAM separates 'what region does the user mean' from 'what class is it'. Trained on enormous mask data, it generalises to unseen object types because it never needed a fixed class vocabulary. That makes it powerful for annotation tooling and as a component in larger systems.

questions.stem: Masks are broadly correct but boundaries are ragged. Which TWO would help?
choices: Train or predict at higher resolution so fine boundary structure survives downsampling
Add a boundary-aware loss term, or refine with a post-processing step that snaps masks to image edges
Increase the batch size
Lower the confidence threshold
questions.explanation: Boundary error concentrates in a thin band of pixels that contributes little to region-overlap losses, so the model is barely penalised for it. Higher resolution preserves the evidence and a boundary-weighted loss makes those pixels matter. Batch size and thresholds do not address boundary quality.

questions.stem: Why can semantic segmentation not count objects?
choices: Its output resolution is too low
It labels pixels by class without distinguishing instances, so two touching objects form one connected region
Counting requires a separate classifier
It only handles one class at a time
questions.explanation: A semantic mask of three adjacent cars is one contiguous blob of car pixels. Connected-component analysis can approximate counting when objects are separated, but fails exactly where it matters — when they touch. Counting needs instance or panoptic segmentation, or detection.

questions.stem: For a 4000x3000 image that will not fit in memory at full resolution, what is the standard segmentation approach?
choices: Downscale to 512x512 and accept the loss
Tile the image into overlapping patches, segment each, and stitch the results — blending the overlap regions to avoid seams
Segment only the centre crop
Convert to grayscale to save memory
questions.explanation: Tiling preserves native resolution, which matters when the targets are small relative to the frame. The overlap exists because tile-edge predictions lack context; blending or discarding the border region of each tile prevents visible seams in the stitched mask.

questions.stem: When augmenting segmentation data, what must be true of the mask?
choices: It should be left unchanged
Every geometric transform applied to the image must be applied identically to the mask, using nearest-neighbour interpolation so class indices are not blended
It should be blurred to match
Only the image needs augmenting
questions.explanation: Masks carry discrete class indices, not intensities. Bilinear interpolation of a mask can produce value 1.5 between class 1 and class 2 — a class that does not exist. Nearest-neighbour preserves valid labels, and any spatial transform must be mirrored exactly or image and mask desynchronise.

questions.stem: What is the practical difference between Dice and IoU as metrics?
choices: They measure different things entirely
They are monotonically related and rank models the same way, but Dice gives a higher number for the same overlap, so they must not be compared across papers
IoU is for boxes, Dice for masks only
Dice ignores false positives
questions.explanation: Dice equals 2·IoU/(1+IoU), so one determines the other and model rankings agree. The numbers differ though — 0.8 Dice corresponds to about 0.67 IoU — which makes cross-paper comparison meaningless unless you check which was reported.

questions.stem: A medical segmentation model has excellent Dice on the training hospital's scans and poor Dice on another hospital's. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The model is too small
Acquisition domain shift: different scanners, protocols and intensity distributions change the input statistics the model learned
The masks are wrong
Dice is the wrong metric
questions.explanation: Scanner vendor, field strength, reconstruction kernel and protocol all shift intensity distributions substantially. Intensity normalisation, augmentation spanning those variations, and multi-site training data are the standard mitigations — and evaluating per site is what exposes the problem at all.

questions.stem: Why does instance segmentation typically cost more compute than semantic segmentation?
choices: Masks are stored at higher precision
It must additionally detect and separate each object, then predict a mask per instance, so cost grows with the number of objects
It requires more classes
It cannot use a backbone
questions.explanation: Semantic segmentation is one dense forward pass regardless of how many objects are present. Instance methods add detection and per-instance mask prediction, so a crowded frame costs substantially more than an empty one — which matters for real-time budgets.

questions.stem: Which TWO indicate that segmentation, rather than detection, is the right task?
choices: The application needs precise object area or shape, such as measuring coverage or defect extent
Objects are amorphous or non-rectangular, so a bounding box is a poor description
The objects need to be counted
Real-time speed is the primary constraint
questions.explanation: Boxes give position and rough extent; masks give shape and exact area. Choose segmentation when the measurement is area or outline, or when a box is a bad fit for the geometry. Counting is served well by detection, and detection is usually the cheaper option when speed dominates.

questions.stem: A binary segmentation model outputs probabilities. How should the threshold be chosen?
choices: Always 0.5
On a validation set, by picking the threshold that optimises the metric that matters for the application — which is rarely exactly 0.5 under class imbalance
By taking the mean probability
It cannot be changed after training
questions.explanation: The default 0.5 assumes balanced classes and symmetric error costs. With a rare foreground, or where a false negative costs far more than a false positive, the optimal threshold moves. Sweeping it on validation and choosing against the real objective is a cheap and frequently skipped gain.
